readerTitle: What a good pilot says during a delay
caseNote: 일상 장면 (비행기 지연) + 가상 사례 (사내 고객지원팀, 호텔 대상 세탁업체) + 실제 연구 (불확실성과 스트레스, 2016)
insight: 위기에서 리더의 일은 답을 갖는 것이 아니라, 답이 나올 때까지 사람들이 기댈 수 있는 일정한 소통 리듬을 주는 것이다.
misconception: 확실한 답이 나올 때까지 기다렸다가 말해야 혼란을 줄일 수 있다. 사람들을 안심시키려면 괜찮다고 말해야 한다.

sources.text: de Berker, A. O. et al. (2016). Computations of uncertainty mediate acute stress responses in humans. Nature Communications, 7, 10996.
US CDC, Crisis and Emergency Risk Communication (CERC) principles: Be first, be right, be credible
비행기, 고객지원팀, 세탁업체 장면은 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: de Berker 외(2016) 연구: 참가자가 바위 밑 뱀(전기 충격) 여부를 예측하는 과제에서 불확실성이 가장 높을 때 스트레스 반응(동공, 피부 전도 등)이 가장 컸다는 결과. 카드 문장 "most stress when they couldn't predict ... more than when they knew it was"가 논문 결과를 과장하지 않는지 게시 전 원문으로 확인하세요.
CDC CERC 원칙 중 "Be first, be right, be credible" 문구가 현재 CDC 자료 표현과 일치하는지 확인하세요.
모든 업무 장면(고객지원팀 15명, 세탁업체 호텔 40곳, 정오 기술자 도착 등)은 설명용 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: The pilot who says "I don't know"
body: Your plane sits at the gate. Forty minutes, no word. Then the captain speaks: "There's a fault with a sensor. We don't know yet how long the fix will take. I'll update you in 15 minutes, even if nothing has changed."
Nothing is fixed. But the cabin relaxes. The captain hasn't solved the problem. She has solved the silence.

image.label: Passengers in a plane cabin listening to an announcement
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 비행기 객실 안, 승객들이 처음엔 굳은 표정이다가 스피커에서 나오는 말풍선("Next update in 15 min")을 듣고 어깨가 풀리는 모습. 실제 항공사 로고나 도장은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The system is down and your team is looking at you.
body: You lead a 15-person support team inside a large company. The company's ordering system went down an hour ago. Phones are ringing. Engineering doesn't know the cause yet.
Your agents ask: what do we tell customers?

options.text: Wait for engineering's answer so you don't spread wrong information
options.feedback: You avoid passing on a mistake, but your agents improvise in the meantime. Fifteen people inventing fifteen stories is its own kind of wrong information.

options.text: Tell the team what you know, what you don't, and that you'll update them at the top of every hour
options.feedback: You can't give them the cause, but you give them a script and a clock. That's most of what they need right now.

options.text: Tell the team it'll be fixed within the hour so customers stay calm
options.feedback: It buys calm for an hour. If the fix takes three, your team has made a promise to hundreds of customers that you then broke.

cards.title: People don't wait quietly. They fill the gap.
body: In a crisis, people don't sit still until the facts arrive. If the leader says nothing, the team hears either "it's worse than we think" or "nobody's in charge."
Rumors move faster than updates, and each person acts on their own guess. The leader who waits for a complete answer often arrives too late. By then, others have already written the story.

cards.title: Lead with rhythm, not answers
body: **Leading in a crisis** starts with a shift: your job is no longer to have the answers. It's to give people something steady while the answers are found.
The simplest tool is a three-part update: **what we know, what we don't know yet, and when you'll hear from me next.** Then keep that promise, even when the update is "no change."

image.label: Three-part update: known, unknown, next update
image.brief: 깔끔한 인포그래픽. 메모 카드 세 칸: "What we know"(체크 아이콘), "What we don't know yet"(물음표), "Next update: 2:00 pm"(시계). 아래에 같은 시계가 일정 간격으로 반복되는 타임라인.

cards.softwareNote: This is why software teams run status pages during outages and post at set times. A regular "still investigating" post tells customers someone is on it, long before the fix exists.

cards.title: Uncertainty can be harder than bad news.
body: In a 2016 study in *Nature Communications*, volunteers showed the most stress when they couldn't predict whether a small electric shock was coming, more than when they knew it was.

A fixed next-update time gives people one small certainty to plan around. Keeping it, time after time, builds the trust you'll need when the real news arrives. Emergency-communication guides, such as the US CDC's, put it simply: **be first, be right, be credible.**

cards.title: Any crisis, in every direction.
body: The same rhythm works for a lost key client, a product recall, a cash crunch or a key person quitting.
It works upward and outward too. Your boss, your clients and your suppliers fill silence the same way your team does.
Notice the contrast with normal times. On a calm week, hourly updates would be noise. The rhythm is a **crisis tool**: it fits when uncertainty is high and people still have to act.

cards.title: Honesty about unknowns has limits.
body: "I don't know" calms people only next to what you *are* doing. "We don't know yet, and here's how we're finding out" helps. A bare "no idea" doesn't.
Don't share guesses as facts, and don't promise update times you can't keep. One missed check-in undoes the trust the rhythm was building.
Finally, end crisis mode on purpose. Tell people when things are back to normal, or the emergency pace becomes the new habit.

cards.title: Now it's a commercial laundry.
body: You run a laundry that washes linens for 40 hotels. At 7 a.m. your main boiler fails. A technician arrives at noon. Hotels expect clean sheets tonight.
What do you do this morning?

options.text: Wait for the technician's diagnosis so you can give clients a real answer
options.feedback: You'd have better facts at noon, but hotels lose the morning they needed to plan. Some may hear about it first from a missing delivery.

options.text: Call clients now: what failed, what you don't know yet, your backup plan, and an update by 1 p.m.
options.feedback: Hotels can't get certainty from you, but they get time to plan. Calling first, with a set next update, protects the relationship even if deliveries slip.

options.text: Reassure clients that deliveries will arrive on time as usual
options.feedback: If the repair works, nobody notices. If it doesn't, 40 hotels learn about the problem and that your word can't be trusted, on the same night.

cards.title: In a crisis, a steady rhythm matters more than a quick answer.
body: Say what you know, what you don't, and when you'll speak next. Then show up on time, every time.
**Try it today:** think of a problem someone is waiting to hear about from you. Send a three-line update: known, unknown, next check-in.
